newsitem.title: UK: EMU likely to start on time - Moody's agency.
newsitem.headline: EMU likely to start on time - Moody's agency.

text.p: Credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday that it was highly probable European monetary union would start on time in 1999, and there was only a small chance of a delay.
"We try to factor in a variety of scenarios, but the highest probability (is) that EMU will go ahead on time," David Levey, co-head of Moody's sovereign risk unit, told Reuters.
Levey's comments followed a detailed study by Moody's on the implications of economic and monetary union for the credit ratings of participating countries.
The U.S. agency concluded that the foreign currency debt ceilings for countries joining EMU would be Aaa, the highest rating possible, signalling the lowest expectation of investment risk.
Moody's said that "together, the potential first-round entrants comprise a net creditor bloc".
This would mean that should countries such as Finland and Belgium enter EMU in the first wave, their foreign currency debt rating ceilings would rise from their present Aa1 to Aaa.

Levey said Moody's was currently "pretty certain" that Finland and Belgium would be two of eight countries in the first wave of EMU. The remaining were likely to be Austria, France, Germany, Netherlands, Ireland and Luxembourg.
He declined comment on Italy, which is also keen to join the first wave, but which has hinted at a German-led campaign to keep it out for the sake of the euro's credibility.
But Levey said British sovereign ratings were unlikely to be affected if the country stayed out of EMU.
"I don't think there's any chance that the UK...will be affected even if stays outside of EMU," Levey said.
Britain, which remains indecisive about whether to commit itself to EMU, currently has Aaa sovereign ratings from Moody's for both its foreign currency and local currency debt.

The introduction of the euro, scheduled for January 1, 1999, has encouraged wide research on the implications for credit risk in European countries. Speculation about the effects of EMU has been a big topic for financial markets as the launch date draws nearer.
The Moody's report follows similar reports from rival rating agencies Standard & Poor's and IBCA last year on EMU.
Levey said the momentum behind the move to a single European currency ensured there was only the smallest probablility that the process would collapse altogether.
"There's a strong dynamic pushing the process forward...but we're not basing our ratings on absolute certainty -- we're hedging our bets," he said.
